title: Generic Container
story: You need to ship three different packages: one holds a number, one holds a text message, one holds a yes/no answer. Instead of building three separate box types, what if you could build ONE box that works with any type? Generics make this possible.
why: Generic types let you write a data structure once and reuse it with any type — Box[Int], Box[Str], Box[Float64] — without duplicating code.
analogy: A generic Box[T] is like a shipping container — the container itself is the same size and shape regardless of what you put inside. Label it 'contains electronics' (Box[Int]) or 'contains books' (Box[Str]) — same box, different contents.
try_it: Add a third type: `Box[Float64]` with 3.14. Then add an `is_empty` method that returns true if the value equals a default. For strings the default is `""`, for Int it's `0`, for Bool it's `false`. How would you write `is_empty` generically? (Hint: you can't easily — different types have different empty concepts! This is a great segway into interfaces in L6.)
tips: `[T]` goes after the type name in both the definition and method signatures: `type Box[T]` and `fn Box.get_value[T]`
Type parameters are filled in at creation time: `Box[Int]{ value: 42 }` — never try to mix types
Generic methods need the type parameter in brackets: `fn Box.set_value[T](self: &mut Box[T], ...)`
common_mistakes: Forgetting `[T]` on method definitions — `fn Box.get_value(self)` won't compile for a generic type
Trying to create a Box without specifying the type: `Box{ value: 42 }` — must be `Box[Int]{ value: 42 }`
Using `T` without declaring it as a type parameter — `[T]` must appear on the type definition first
